title: The Najdorf
summary: One rook pawn, and the race it starts

steps.title: A Pawn Move With a Library Behind It
steps.text:
Black's fifth move here goes to a rook pawn that attacks nothing, defends nothing and brings out nothing. It is also one of the most analyzed moves in chess, with a shelf of theory behind it and no sign of the shelf getting shorter.

Miguel Najdorf played it as a life's work and the variation carries the name. Fischer and Kasparov then made it the sharpest answer to 1.e4 in the world.

So the question is what a pawn on the rim can possibly be worth.

steps.title: The Push Black Actually Wants
steps.text:
What Black wants is the e-pawn two squares forward, throwing the knight out of the middle and taking a real share of it.

Try that right now and watch what answers: {{e5}} {{Bb5+}}. The check comes first and everything else waits. Black has six legal replies to it — a knight to d7 or c6, the bishop or queen dropped onto d7, or a king that moves and never castles.

The push is right. The move order is not.

steps.title: Three Pieces, One Square
steps.text:
Count what reaches b5 from here. The knight on d4 jumps to it. The knight on c3 jumps to it. The bishop on f1 has an empty road — e2, d3, c4 — that arrives on b5 with check.

Three pieces, one square, and that square is the whole reason the center push has to wait a move.

One quiet pawn step covers b5 and answers all three at once. Nothing is developed by it and no threat is made. A door is closed before anyone walks through it.

steps.prompt: Take b5 away from both white knights and the bishop, before you go anywhere near the center.
steps.hint: Only one black pawn can guard b5, and it gets there in a single step without leaving the edge file.

steps.title: What the Pawn Bought
steps.text:
Now the same push arrives with nothing attached to it: {{Be3}} {{e5}} {{Nb3}} {{Be6}}.

The knight goes backward to b3 rather than forward to b5, and Black owns a center pawn on e5 with a bishop out behind it.

The bill is real. Pushing the e-pawn leaves a hole on d5 that no black pawn can ever guard again, and White will spend the next several moves trying to park a piece on it. Black pays it anyway. One square against a share of the middle is a trade worth making.

steps.title: Opposite Wings
steps.text:
By move ten both kings have run, White's to c1 and Black's to g8. That one fact changes what a pawn is for.

Pawns are shelter only where your own king is standing. On the far wing they are soldiers, and nobody needs them at home. So White sends the g-pawn and the h-pawn at g8, Black sends the a-pawn and the b-pawn at c1, and neither side stops to defend.

A defensive move here is a move handed to the opponent.

steps.title: Counting the Race
steps.text:
Material is the wrong unit now. Count moves to the enemy king instead: how many pushes until a line opens onto it, and who arrives first.

White's g-pawn has two steps to make before the knight on f6 is kicked and the g-file starts to crack. Black's b-pawn has two steps to reach b4, where the knight on c3 — the piece standing in front of White's king — has to answer.

Same count, and Black is on move.

> On opposite wings you are not counting pawns, you are counting moves.

steps.prompt: Start the queenside race with the pawn whose next two steps evict the knight guarding White's king.
steps.hint: Exactly one of your pawns can stand on b4 in two moves, and nothing on the board is stopping it.
